articles.title: The Class Divide Haunting Climate Politics
articles.author: Matt Huber
articles.content: Socialists believe the working class is the key agent of social transformation in a capitalist society. So, perhaps the most important problem for socialists today is the fact that significant swaths of the working-class are shifting to the populist right — not just in the United States but all over the world . A new report from Joan C. Williams and Jared Abbott, The Left’s Coalition Crisis , explains how working-class views in the US diverge sharply from the views of the educated and affluent liberals and progressives that increasingly dominate the Democratic party coalition — a party that the American working class once saw as their natural home. This divergence has grown so wide — and the Democratic Party so deeply unpopular — that in many parts of the country there is a “ Democratic penalty ,” where candidates can expect losing sizable support by merely being associated with the party’s brand. As the Center for Working-Class Politics newsletter summarized it, “A key finding of this report is that college-educated liberals live in a class bubble where virtually everyone agrees with them on culture and climate issues — but working-class people don’t.” The report is specifically interested in comparing the class gap between upper-middle-class liberals — people with college degrees who vote or lean Democratic and who have household incomes in the top 25 percent of the distribution — and a specific portion of the US working class defined as “the group that has veered far right . . . middle-status voters.” This group is specified as non-college-graduate households in the middle 50 percent of the income distribution, making between roughly $40,000 and $100,000 per year. The report covers the class gap on a wide variety of issues including immigration, public safety, and abortion rights, but one of the most polarizing issues is climate change. Williams and Abbott write: Liberal college grads run 29 points more supportive of climate change initiatives than working-class respondents — the fourth-largest class gap we found (87% vs. 58%). There is a 20-point prioritization gap: working-class Americans ranked climate change as only their 27th priority (out of 30); liberal college grads ranked it 15th. Dig deeper by race, and it’s clear that only one group ranks climate change highly as an issue — white liberal college grads (ranked sixth compared to twenty-seventh for the white working class). Even black and Latino college grads don’t rank it highly (twenty-second and twenty-third out of thirty respectively). Given the scale of what’s required to address climate change, surely requiring large supermajorities to accomplish the boldest action, these numbers should raise alarm bells. Bur rather than despair, the report bluntly asserts, “Given that climate change is not a working-class priority, advocates need to link it to something that is.” And they have good ideas on how to do that. But first, we should understand what kinds of climate ideas and policies repel working-class support in the first place. Don’t Give Right-Wing Populists Ammunition One of the most frustrating aspects of climate politics today is that it is arguably the Right that mobilizes class politics most effectively on this issue. Right-wing politicians consistently argue climate action is a plot of the liberal elite to harm the lives of average working-class families with rising energy costs and lost jobs. On the other hand, liberal activists often make climate change about everything but class — “ Believe Science ” — and sometimes advocating policies like carbon taxes that would raise the price of energy (affirming precisely what the Right warns against). The report throws this problem into sharp relief. A question asking about a carbon tax that would impose an additional $40/month on consumers obtains 69 percent support from elite liberals, while working-class support is a paltry 24 percent! Meanwhile, simply reframing the tax to focus on emitters with no increase in household costs increases working-class support to 65 percent (and support from liberal college grads to 90 percent). While climate activism tends to single out the fossil fuel industry as the enemy, often targeting “Big Oil” in particular, one of the key findings is that this kind of politics falls flat with working people: “Climate action to rein in Big Oil produces the widest class gap, with support from 91% of liberal college grads versus just 50% working class support — a 41-point gap.” This might be because most working-class people understand they rely on fossil fuels for their basic everyday existence — to drive to work, to heat their homes, and more — and as we’ve seen with rising gas and electricity prices as of late, these costs impose significant burdens on already strained household budgets. A politics narrowly aimed against the fossil fuel industry will struggle to overcome the industry’s own highly misleading narrative that they are the key to delivering affordable energy to American families. Another topic beloved by affluent liberals is the commitment to the Paris Agreement — a nonbinding climate agreement signed by 195 countries in 2015. Not only does the Right paint this as a globalist plan meant to impinge on US national interests, but the treaty itself also translates into an abstract politics of degree targets and emission-cut commitments. Unsurprisingly, there is a massive class gap over whether the US should stay in the treaty: liberal college grads oppose withdrawal at a level of 95 percent, but the working class only shows 39 percent opposition. There are other topics climate activists should avoid entirely. For good or ill, the electric vehicle (EV) is cemented in the popular imagination as an overly expensive vehicle for the smug elite ; thus working-class support for government incentives to purchase EVs (not even mandates) is abysmal at 37 percent (compared to 66 percent for liberal college grads). But even left-wing climate advocates get squeamish around the idea of an EV-focused transition. One thing the report did not ask is whether there is a class gap on questions of public transit — which, in cities at least, is disproportionately relied on by the working class. Of course, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made expanding free public transit a cornerstone of his campaign, a policy that would have a positive climate impact as well. Meet the Working Class at the “End of the Month” The report not only shows the extent of the class gap on a number of climate questions but also demonstrates how reframing the issues can dramatically increasing working-class support for pro-climate policy. If the message shifts focus from “Big Oil” to “corporate profiteers,” working-class support increases by 12 percentage points. This is no doubt due to the simmering popular anger toward the rich in general, rather than the fossil fuel industry in particular. The most dramatic gains come, unsurprisingly, from a focus on what matters to working-class people every day: energy costs, well-paying jobs, and even pollution. A message emphasizing those issues resonated with an impressive 75 percent of working-class respondents while retaining 90 percent of affluent college-grad liberals. This finding aligns with a core slogan of the Yellow Vests movement in France, when it complained that the political class only cares about the “end of the world” when workers are trying to make it to the “end of the month.” Indeed, while climate change itself can appear gradual and abstract, it has been the consistent failure of climate advocacy to reach people at this “end of the month” level. The report also shows the working-class responds positively — increasing 17 points — to a “Build, Baby, Build” message that centers economic growth, job creation, and calls for reshoring manufacturing. It should be obvious why this framing resonates in communities destroyed by decades of free trade and deindustrialization. But this message also stands in contrast to the last two decades of climate activism that has had a skewed focus on blocking destructive fossil fuel projects like pipelines or coal-fired power. While many of these struggles are inspiring — the fight over the Dakota Access Pipeline comes to mind — this style of politics inevitably antagonizes unions and workers in these industries who we need to build and replace all that fossil fuel infrastructure with clean energy alternatives. The report shows the wider working class is more aligned with these building trades unions. One possible response is that the Democrats already tried a “Build, Baby, Build” strategy, linking climate to jobs with the Inflation Reduction Act, which led us right back to Donald Trump. But crucially, the report advises we “don’t throw out the baby with the bathwater” on that front. Not only had many IRA projects barely gotten off the ground before Trump was reelected, but studies have shown the tax-credit model of policymaking made it difficult for communities to link any economic benefits to a coherent political project of the Biden administration. (It didn’t help that Joe Biden himself was incapable of communicating those connections.) While Marxists and others on the Left are correct to point out that many college-educated progressives are themselves part of the working class — even many lawyers and doctors must work for a paycheck to survive, after all — the key to socialist political strategy is uniting the whole working-class around a majoritarian agenda. For a civilizational challenge like shifting away from fossil fuels, only broad-based working-class power is capable of achieving what planetary systems require. To build that power, we need to understand why we are failing to win many workers to our politics, and how we can change that.

articles.title: Socialists Are Out-Organizing the Democratic Establishment
articles.author: Cole Sansom
articles.content: In the weeks following the resounding electoral victory of the New York City Democratic Socialists of America (NYC-DSA) this past June, the Democratic establishment’s complaints appeared right on schedule. This time, in addition to the expected accusations of radicalism, antisemitism, and, of course, anti-Americanism, came a new line of attack: the organization is taking advantage of the Democratic Party.Former Democratic National Committee chair Jaime Harrison, best known for twice setting new election campaign spending records only to lose both times, had this to say:If you hate the Democratic Party, then please don’t run for our nomination. Don’t use our resources. Don’t rely on our volunteers. Don’t use our infrastructure. Don’t ask Democrats to invest their time, money, and energy in your campaign. Focus on building the party you actually support. Political parties aren’t perfect, but they’re built by millions of people who knock doors, make calls, organize meetings, and fight for the values they believe in. If you don’t believe in the party, then don’t ask its members to carry you across the finish line.For anyone who has experienced working with the Democratic Party, some confusion is more than justified. Which volunteers does Harrison refer to? And what infrastructure?Does he mean the few software resources that NYC-DSA campaigns pay to use (and face frequent delays and interruptions using)? Or maybe access to ActBlue, the Democratic fundraising platform? I struggle to think of any national or local Democratic organizations we could plunder for volunteers.In fact, Harrison’s descriptions of “people who knock doors, make calls, organize meetings, and fight for the values they believe in” is a far more fitting descriptor of NYC-DSA’s electoral program than anything to be found among the Democratic Party’s establishment and its elected officials and candidates.In this critique, DSA’s success running on the Democratic ballot line is commonly framed through the metaphor of “parasite and host,” recently by the Atlantic’s James Kirchik. The comparison, however, rests on the assumption of an organism that can be preyed upon.At the state level, where NYC-DSA has found most success, it is unclear what the party, whose weak efforts in 2022 arguably caused Democrats to lose the House, could offer. And Harrison’s diatribe implies an easily susceptible voter base who have been duped by hateful actors. Nowhere do these polemicists against socialism ever admit the possibility that the voters themselves may have made a decision to support NYC-DSA candidates, based on agreeing with those candidates on the issues.This casual disregard for the general populace is what many in NYC-DSA’s Electoral Working Group consider a key point of divergence from the mainstream establishment. The project was born not through lack of access to large donor checks (although that does play a part) but instead a desire to build a political system that is in fact, genuinely small-‘d’ democratic.The core of this is that, to quote NYC-DSA cochair Grace Mausser, “volunteers [are] the centerpiece” of these campaigns. Staff provide the infrastructural support and consistent presence to build a volunteer program so that anyone from the community can walk into a campaign office and not only have their voice heard but become an active player in setting the political direction of that campaign. As a result, these campaigns do not simply reflect communities but actively construct them.This is in stark contrast to the traditional methods of Democratic campaigns. As Tascha van Auken, one of the architects of NYC-DSA’s electoral program, told Jacobin: “You can talk to people who’ve worked on run-of-the-mill, mainstream campaigns outside of DSA; the culture is really bad. People don’t feel respected.” In these campaigns, door-knocking and other voter contact is seen as irrelevant, a sideshow; television and digital advertising are considered the campaigns’ main functions.This situation benefits consultants while leaving those without the means to donate the increasingly enormous amounts required to run an ad-heavy campaign out in the lurch. As a result, working people become further removed from those that seek to represent them; increasing levels of mediation contribute to a political culture that is alienated from anyone but the very wealthy, who are able to access politicians in person, not just through a screen.This leads to the Democratic Party as it exists today, out of step and out of contact with its voter base. In this environment, NYC-DSA’s electoral project has the opportunity not simply to score some victories but to build the kind of organizing networks that will be necessary to create the just and equitable society that we envision.This is not an easy feat, as the Electoral Working Group discovered this year in coordinating across many overlapping campaigns: creating cohesive messaging, field programs, and downballot door-knocking that does not leave any candidate underrepresented is extremely difficult work.In particular, our campaign for Claire Valdez in New York’s Seventh Congressional District, required coordination across five insurgent state campaigns and a similar number of incumbents running for reelection. A typical Democratic party operation would have run these campaigns separately, with a party committee allocating resources (on a federal, state, or countywide level) and otherwise stepping back and letting staff run their operations or outsourcing to political action committees (PACs).Instead, we did the hard legwork of making decisions across those campaigns that would benefit us all, resulting in a slate that won handily across Brooklyn and Queens. (Our single loss, Conrad Blackburn in Harlem, faced extraordinary outside spending and coordination challenges early on.) While congressional candidates more easily gain media attention, NYC-DSA’s approach allows those media appearances to function as an entry point, to learn more about downballot candidates and get involved in their races.Among our campaigns, the level of skills acquired and practiced, along with the extensive spectrum of electoral work that numerous volunteers took part in, was humbling. In one assembly race, David Orkin’s, the candidate’s team filed a petitioning challenge against an opponent. The campaign staff encouraged volunteers — many of whom had never worked on an electoral campaign previously — to learn the ins and outs of electoral regulation, becoming experts in the procedures.During this process, we came to a realization: we were not somehow “hacking” the country’s electoral system. On the contrary, we were the only ones actually doing the work properly, following the rules and regulations to the letter and winning without the help of billionaires, professional consultants, or connections to the judicial or electoral institutions.NYC-DSA has never won a race simply by duping a shallow-minded electorate, as the commentariat would have you believe. Rather, we have consistently practiced the hard work of building a democratic coalition, a volunteer base, digital and physical infrastructure, and the institutional knowledge required to win elections and form a politically engaged populace. We did not steal these techniques from the Democratic Party, for there is nothing there to steal (if there ever was, it has not existed since 2008). The alliances we built, with working-class community organizations such as Desis Rising Up and Moving and CAAAV: Organizing Asian Communities, were built upon mutual trust that had to be won, not transacted.The way campaigns are run can reflect the politics they aim to produce to the world. The professionalized campaigns considered the norm by the Democratic Party elites conceive of the voting blocs of their alliance as top-down bodies, where single voices can command distinct demographic blocs; these elites are the medium through which voters are reached.I experienced this myself during a season working on a mainstream Democratic campaign. More than half a decade on, I cannot get out of my head the words of my boss, a consultant who ran field campaigns for mainstream Dems: “They’re going to do everything they can to avoid knocking doors.” With a field operation run on advanced surveillance rather than generosity, what message were they putting out to the world?NYC-DSA’s campaigns are built on repetition of our smallest unit: the conversation at the door. Our society encourages isolation and seeing others either as potential dangers or potential consumers; with every conversation, our volunteers are not only helping the campaign achieve victory but breaking down the barriers that keep us apart. Our tight volunteer infrastructure program is not only a model for the future of left-electoral campaigns but a part of the path toward winning the world we want to build.The Democratic Party’s alienation from their voters is both cause and effect of the party’s capture by elites. In its current form, it not only lacks large volunteer networks and infrastructure — it is fundamentally unable to create them. Doing so would require advancing a form of politics that would reconnect not only with the needs of working people but also with working people themselves. That would mean, essentially, becoming DSA.

articles.title: Mass funeral held in Gaza, largest in history of Palestinian cause
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: On Tuesday, August 4, thousands of Palestinians gathered in the Sabra neighborhood of Gaza City to bid farewell to 112 members of the Al-Hasayneh and Abu Sharia families before they were finally laid to rest, almost three years after their tragic deaths. This includes 40 children, 38 women, and seven people with disabilities. The victims of the two families, who come from one extended clan, were killed in Israeli airstrikes that flattened their residential block in Sabra on November 23, 2023. According to estimations, the massacre resulted in the killing of at least 308 people. However, less than half of the bodies and remains of all the victims were retrieved after 136 hours of digging through the wreckage. The Palestinian Civil Defense said that its teams were unable to find 157 bodies still missing under the rubble, with some remains expected to have fused with concrete and rebar or vanished under the intense pressure of the explosions. While the largest since the beginning of Israel’s genocidal aggression on Gaza, this funeral is not the only one of its kind. Nor will it be the last, as Israel continues to launch assaults on Gaza and prevent rescue teams from carrying out recovery operations. For almost three years, Palestinians in Gaza have not only endured all types of brutal death at the hands of Israeli Forces, but also have not been able to recover the bodies and remains of their loved ones. Read more: Being bombed, starved to death, or killed while seeking food: Israel’s options for Palestinians in Gaza The scene of crowds bidding farewell to members of the same family , friends, or neighbors at a joint funeral has become familiar to Palestinians in both Gaza and the occupied West Bank over the last few decades. Palestinians in both areas say the international community has stood idly by while Israel continues its atrocities.

articles.title: NUMSA court victory opens path to save jobs at Ekapa Mine in South Africa
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa (NUMSA) has secured a legal victory after the Kimberley High Court suspended the liquidation of Ekapa Minerals and placed the diamond mining company under business rescue; a ruling the union says offers renewed hope to thousands of workers facing unemployment. The judgment, delivered on July 27, 2026, by Acting Judge T. Tyuthuza, halted the company’s provisional liquidation and appointed an interim Business Rescue Practitioner to oversee efforts aimed at restoring the financially distressed mining company while preserving jobs and economic activity. NUMSA described the ruling as “a decisive victory for the working class over cold corporate indifference,” saying that workers’ lives and livelihoods should take precedence over corporate interests. The union also paid tribute to the five miners who lost their lives in the catastrophic mudslide at Ekapa Mine in February, describing the tragedy as a painful reminder of the dangers faced by mineworkers and extending solidarity to the victims’ families. Read more: South African police attack and arrest striking workers at Ekapa diamond mines Workers challenge liquidation through the courts The dispute began after Ekapa announced in March 2026 that it had applied for provisional liquidation. NUMSA opposed the decision, criticizing management for pursuing liquidation without consulting either the union or government while workers were still mourning colleagues killed in the mine disaster. According to the union, more than 1,000 employees were left without salaries for months and over 300 workers were subjected to unilateral layoffs. NUMSA argued that business rescue, rather than liquidation, offered the best opportunity to preserve employment and protect the local economy. In its ruling, the High Court affirmed NUMSA’s stance as the majority trade union to seek business rescue, suspended the liquidation proceedings, and rejected arguments by the company and liquidators that the mine had no viable future. The court accepted evidence that the February mudslide had affected only a specific section of the underground workings and that significant operational areas, including Wesselton, surface mining operations, and several underground levels remained commercially viable. High Court finds business rescue a better alternative The court further found that liquidation would have resulted in substantial destruction of value, including the automatic loss of the mine’s valuable mining rights. Instead, business rescue would preserve those rights, enable the recovery of more than R400 million owed to the company by related entities, secure R25 million in post-commencement finance, and create the possibility of maintaining mining operations while restructuring the business. The proposed rescue plan also envisages preserving approximately 500 jobs immediately and delivering better returns to creditors than liquidation. NUMSA: Workers hold the key to the mine’s future Speaking after the judgment, Tshepiso Mochabela from NUMSA’s Regional Legal Office in Kimberley told BreakThrough News that the most direct significance of the ruling is that it gives workers a chance to keep their jobs. “The immediate consequence of this judgment is that it creates a pathway for workers to return to work. By suspending the liquidation proceedings and placing Ekapa under Business Rescue, the court has preserved the opportunity for mining operations to resume under the supervision of the Business Rescue Practitioner. For hundreds of workers and their families, this judgment restores hope where liquidation would have meant the immediate loss of employment.” Looking beyond the immediate relief, Mochabela said NUMSA’s objective is to ensure that every worker affected by the crisis ultimately returns to employment if the rescue process succeeds. He explained that business rescue is intended not only to stabilize financially distressed companies but also to preserve productive enterprises and protect livelihoods wherever there is a realistic prospect of recovery. According to Mochabela, NUMSA’s success before the court rested on presenting a credible, evidence-based alternative to liquidation. He emphasized that workers themselves played a decisive role in developing the rescue proposal by contributing their practical knowledge of the mine’s operations. “Their experience demonstrated that the mudslide had been confined to one section of the mine while substantial operations remained viable,” he said, adding that this knowledge, combined with the work of the Business Rescue Practitioner and NUMSA’s legal team, persuaded the court that there was a reasonable prospect of rescuing the business. Mochabela argued that the judgment reinforces the importance of organized labor in corporate restructuring. Read more: NUMSA urges alternative industrialization path to save South Africa’s manufacturing as Goodyear exits “This judgment demonstrates that workers are not merely employees, they are custodians of institutional knowledge and key stakeholders in the future of the enterprise. Their experience proved invaluable in showing that the mine was worth saving,” he said. He added that the decision shows how collaboration between workers, organized labor, and business rescue professionals can provide a viable legal mechanism for preserving jobs, protecting economic value, and giving distressed companies an opportunity to recover. Following the judgment, NUMSA has called on the company’s management and liquidators to cooperate fully as the rescue process begins.

articles.title: Far right exploits Ceuta incident to call for border crackdown
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: At least 88 people died during a mass crossing from Morocco into Ceuta, a North Africa territory administered by Spain, late last week. According to local reports, over 65,000 people entered Ceuta on July 30-31. The event was weaponized by far-right and right-wing groups worldwide to criticize Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s administration, while progressives warned such events are bound to increase under the European Union’s increasingly dehumanized approach to migration. Last week’s images show thousands of people stranded in Ceuta, many having arrived without any belongings. Grassroots organizations providing support to migrants in the area emphasized that people were left for hours without access to water or food as Spanish authorities scrambled to coordinate a response. Instead, local residents organized to ensure access to essential supplies, No Name Kitchen reported on social media. Right-wing groups claimed the mass crossing was the result of the Sánchez administration’s migration policy, which they described as lax, arguing it lays the groundwork for an “invasion” of both Spain and the rest of Europe. Santiago Abascal , leader of the far-right party Vox, repeated these accusations over recent days, stating that Morocco had orchestrated an invasion that the Spanish government was attempting to cover up. He also spoke in favor of border militarization. While militarization and violent crackdowns stand at the core of the EU’s migration strategy, the Sánchez administration has taken a different approach, recently facilitating regularization for thousands of undocumented migrants. While this has not meant a clean break with harmful EU policy frameworks, it signaled a potential alternative course – much needed in a region whose major economies could become entirely right-wing dominated in upcoming elections. Read more: Insurgent left candidate may spoil far right’s plans in 2027 French presidential election Vox’s narrative was echoed by far-right organizations across the region, while Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced a temporary reintroduction of stricter travel checks from Spain. Meloni’s administration has spearheaded the EU’s most recent migration governance framework, which includes curbs to the right to asylum and establishing “return hubs” in third countries for “irregular” migrants. These concepts were recently introduced at the bloc level through legislation related to the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum. Recent reports signal Italian authorities will push for their expansion following the events in Ceuta. Notably, the right also used the mass crossing to claim that migration to Europe is increasingly being used as a tool of “geopolitical coercion,” insisting the only solution is to introduce even harsher policies. In an opinion piece published Tuesday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis went as far as to call for a mechanism that would allow EU members to “temporarily” suspend asylum applications for those who arrive in mass migration waves deemed to be coordinated with the intention of exerting pressure on Europe. “This is not a departure from Europe’s values but a necessary adaptation to new realities,” Mitsotakis wrote – and he was essentially not lying, seeing that this would be a logical step forward in the policy direction endorsed by EU members. Read more: EU’s new migration framework foreshadows dehumanization and human rights violation Gleeful reactions came from outside Europe as well, including from the Trump administration and Israeli authorities. US Vice President JD Vance wrote on social media that “images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West.” Meanwhile, Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir wrote that Prime Minister Sánchez should “open the doors of Spain and grant refuge to the residents of Gaza who seek to emigrate.” The Sánchez administration has been among the few European countries calling out the ongoing genocide in Gaza and mounting resistance to pressure coming from the US, including in the case of its war on Iran . As a result, US President Donald Trump has described the Spanish government as “very bad” on multiple occasions, threatening to sever trade relations. Some analyses have pondered whether US and Israeli involvement in the events in Ceuta expands further than social media posts, especially considering the material relations both established with Morocco . Read more: ICE killings fuel nationwide protests In the days following the mass crossing, criticism of Moroccan authorities mounted in the center and left of the European political camp as well, with claims that they made no effort to prevent the events or minimize the ensuing chaos. But while progressive organizations recognized that under the current migration regime Morocco has the space to manipulate migration paths to pressure governments like Spain’s, they insisted on a radically different approach from the one suggested by Mitsotakis. “It is precisely Europe’s neocolonial migration policy – supported by both the right and the center-left – that has placed this geopolitical weapon in Morocco’s hands,” Italian left party Potere al Popolo emphasized. “European countries are erecting walls and barriers against migrants everywhere, and then they finance and support dictatorships or semi-dictatorships with billions of euros to manage these flows on our behalf.” “The difference between the right and the center-left is that the former uses this system to spread propaganda while managing it; the center-left manages it quietly,” they added. “This system, however, cannot be reformed; it cannot be managed. It is up to us workers to organize ourselves to tear it down together and build a new system based on international solidarity and equal rights.”

articles.title: El Niño to exacerbate hunger crisis in Africa, warn international agencies
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: The strongest El Niño in 75 years, brewing in the Pacific Ocean, casts a dark shadow over Africa as crop failures, water shortages, and other disasters loom over the continent that is home to 309 million of the 645 million who suffered hunger globally last year.​ Read more: Over half of Africa’s population suffered from food insecurity: UN report A climate pattern caused by periodic warming of surface water temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, El Niño disrupts atmospheric circulation, causing droughts, floods, and extreme temperatures worldwide. Its impacts are particularly acute as the planet is already warming due to greenhouse emissions.​ Meteorologists have forecasted that the moderate El Niño, already at work in the Pacific by July, will peak between November 2026 and February 2027, with a 90% probability that it will develop into what has been termed a “Super El Niño.”​ “The 2026/2027 El Niño event is projected to be the strongest since 1950. This is not a distant possibility. It is an imminent risk that demands immediate preparation,” said Moses Vilakati, the African Union (AU) commissioner for Agriculture, Rural Development, Blue Economy and Sustainable Environment (ARBE).​ Addressing an extraordinary session of the Specialized Technical Committee on Agriculture, Rural Development, Water and Environment on July 27, he insisted, “The question before us is no longer whether another El Niño will occur. The scientific evidence suggests that it will. Africa needs to be sufficiently prepared to anticipate, mitigate and respond effectively to its impacts.” The uneven impact across the continent complicates the response. Its impact on Western and Central Africa is unpredictable, and will vary between areas within the region. In Southern Africa, El Niño is associated with a shortage of rain during the principal agricultural season between October and April. The transition from drought-resistant millets and tubers to maize as the main staple food under colonialism has made the region highly vulnerable to crop failure and shortages.​ The worst impact is expected on Eastern Africa. El Niño has historically spelt poor harvests due to reduced rainfall in its western parts, including Sudan and South Sudan (two of the hungriest countries in the world) and parts of Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Uganda.​ Oxfam distributing clean water to a drought-stricken area in southern Ethiopia during 2011 drought. Photo: Wikimedia Commons In the eastern part of the Horn of Africa, flash floods and landslides caused by excessive rains and overflowing rivers between October and December threaten to destroy crops, damage homes and infrastructure, and displace communities. The consequences are particularly dire for Somalia, which also remains one of the hungriest countries in the world. “These climate extremes have profound consequences for agriculture, food security, water resources, energy production, public health, education, infrastructure and ultimately the livelihoods of millions of Africans,” Harsen Nyambe, director for sustainable environment and blue economy at the AU Commission, told the extraordinary session last week. “Now is the time to act: mitigating risks before impacts are felt, rather than waiting for emergency response after the fact,” insisted the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Along with the World Food Program (WFP), it has issued “a joint Anticipatory Action Appeal seeking USD 202 million to protect 8.8 million people” across 22 countries, including 12 in Africa. However, heavily dependent on the US for their funds, the agencies are already fund-starved by the administration of President Donald Trump. The WFP reported a 40% slash in its funding from 2024 to 2025.

articles.title: “Department of Injustice”: Norm Eisen on Todd Blanche AG Nom, Reflecting Pool Vandalism Case
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : Well, later in the broadcast, we’re going to go to an exhibit about to open in Chicago about the life and death of Emmett Till. But first, this top news: Todd Blanche’s nomination to become the next attorney general appears to be back on track after Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina said they will now support his confirmation. On Sunday, Blanche issued a written order that purports to rescind a $1.8 billion so-called anti-weaponization fund, what many call a slush fund, that was part of a controversial settlement of Trump’s personal lawsuit against the IRS . Blanche also said in writing the immunity agreement Trump struck with the IRS applies only retroactively. But critics say there are major loopholes in Blanche’s written assurances. The Senate Judiciary Committee is voting on Blanche’s nomination today. Blanche, who is Trump’s former personal defense attorney, first told senators, “We are not moving forward with the fund,” during a hearing last month. ACTING ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE : We are not moving forward with the fund, period. We — the reasons for the fund is something that President Trump talked about for a long time, which is the fact that there were a lot of people in this country who had their government weaponized against them. The reasons for the fund, I think, were — remain as important as they were before, but we are not moving forward with the fund. AMY GOODMAN : That’s what he said. But until this weekend, he didn’t put it in writing. And we’ll find out if the writing matters. This comes as U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro Friday dropped the case against the former U.S. Olympian canoeist Davey Hearn, accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. On June 19th, Hearn stopped by the pool while on a 64-mile bike ride. He says he touched the pool to see what it felt like and was then arrested, handcuffed, held for five hours by U.S. Park Police. He was then charged with a felony. Prosecutors in Washington also dropped charges against three others who were similarly accused of damaging the pool. President Trump, in response, blasted the U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, who said the damage to the Reflecting Pool was ultimately due to poor construction and not to vandalism as Trump had claimed for months. In her filing, Pirro blamed the Department of Interior, DOI , for failing to provide accurate documentation on the case before her office wrote the indictment. Pirro said her office had received new information showing the damage was, quote, “the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI ,” unquote. Pirro also blamed Trump over his demands to finish the pool’s renovation by the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence on July Fourth. She said, “The rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work that was not remediated before the project was finished and the fencing removed. … Given all this newly discovered information, it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism,” unquote. The filing contradicted Pirro’s initial claim that there was “tremendous evidence” of vandalism. Meanwhile, CNN spoke to sources who said Trump was furious and considering removing Pirro as U.S. attorney. Trump met with Pirro at the White House Monday. He spoke from the Oval Office. PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : That was the one mistake with the Reflecting Pool, and they hadn’t put up the cameras yet. They had enough up, because you see what’s happening. But if they would have had them up, we would have had a lot of — it would have been a lot easier. But — and I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed with Jeanine Pirro. She — she folded like an umbrella. And people get away with things, and it’s a disgrace. AMY GOODMAN : For more, we go to Washington, D.C., where we’re joined by Norm Eisen, co-founder and executive chair of Democracy Defenders Fund, one of Davey Hearn’s attorneys. He was White House special counsel for ethics and government reform in the Obama administration, considered Obama’s ethics adviser. Welcome back to Democracy Now! , Norm. We last had you on when Davey was charged. Now the charges have been dropped. I want to talk about both Davey Hearn and Blanche, Blanche now signing this statement that some say is actually not worth too much, that Trump could re-sign an executive order almost immediately around getting rid of the $1.8 million slush fund, and the whole question of Trump being audited retroactively, his tax returns, his children’s and his businesses’. Why don’t you start there? NORM EISEN : Well, Amy, at Democracy Defenders Fund, we represent 35 former federal judges, appointed by presidents of both parties, who filed in the federal district court in Florida, Judge Williams, that oversaw the underlying dispute that gave rise to the slush fund and the associated purported releases for Donald Trump and his family. And the judges made the point that there’s no case or controversy. It’s not a real dispute between Donald Trump and the federal government. And under the Constitution, you have to have a dispute in order to have a slush fund or in order to have these kinds of releases. The judge, in response to our papers, found that there was no legal basis for this, ordered that you can’t even refer to these documents, including the one Blanche signed, as settlements. And we’re continuing to litigate that. So, we have profound concerns about the whole mess. We’re going to keep going in court. And it just is not right to take this $1.8 billion, to try to take it away from the American people. And then, the additional documents filed by Mr. Blanche with the Senate don’t really materially change the fundamental illegality of the whole thing. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Well, what about this whole issue that what has survived is this retroactive immunity for Trump and his sons and the Trump Organization on any tax charges or investigations? NORM EISEN : The releases, supposed releases, can’t be valid if there was never an underlying claim or controversy, a constitutional basis to start the case. It’s just a giveaway to the president. It’s a shock that our Department of Justice would engage in that behavior. These documents that Mr. Blanche filed with the Senate don’t really change that. And we’re going to keep on going in court to make sure that this is never acted upon. I think if Donald Trump ever tried to use that to say, “Hey, I got a release,” courts could throw it out. They could refuse to recognize it. The whole thing is an example, one of the worst examples, of the corruption of the Trump administration. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And could you talk in general about the role of Todd Blanche since he was named attorney general? NORM EISEN : Well, it’s been profoundly concerning. There have been a series of offenses against the rule of law, miscarriages of justice. And we saw that with the wrongful prosecutions of Tish James, of Jim Comey, David Huerta, the labor leader in California. I was part of that defense team. That case was just thrown out. He was prosecuted for peacefully protesting. They had to drop that case. And that, of course, brings us to the case of Mr. Hearn. Of all of the things that we can say about the Department of Justice, the single worst thing that it has done under Todd Blanche’s leadership is go after innocent people. That’s the opposite of justice, should be called the Department of Injustice. AMY GOODMAN : So, what happens with Davey Hearn now? And can other charges be brought? And do you think U.S. Attorney Pirro is out? NORM EISEN : Well, the latest reporting after yesterday’s meeting was that she had not offered her resignation. Her resignation had not been requested at that meeting. We’ll see if that turns out to be the case. Look, Davey Hearn was innocent. We’ve said so from the very beginning of this case. The Department of Justice knew he was innocent. We started filing a series of motions the day after the arraignment. We filed one with before-and-after pictures based on the government’s own evidence, showing that the Reflecting Pool was unchanged after Mr. Hearn touched it. It was the same before as it was after. So, it’s appropriate that the Department of Justice has requested the court to drop the charges. I think it would be pretty tough, also terribly wrong, to charge Mr. Hearn again, after the admissions that the Department of Justice has made in their filing at the end of last week that they can’t establish proof beyond a reasonable doubt, that they don’t have evidence that the damage that they claimed actually happened, that the cause of the damage to the Reflecting Pool was a botched and rushed renovation. AMY GOODMAN : And let’s remember, this botched and — NORM EISEN : So, we’re going to — AMY GOODMAN : Let’s remember, this botched renovation was as a result of a no-bid contract given to a friend of President Trump. Norm Eisen, we’re going to leave it there, co-founder and executive chair of Democracy Defenders Fund, one of Davey Hearn’s attorneys, was White House special counsel for ethics and government reform in the Obama administration. Coming up, Emmett Till would have turned 85 on July 25th. What if Emmett Till lived. We’ll speak with cultural historian Sarah Elizabeth Lewis. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Sweet Honey in the Rock, “Down by the Riverside,” performing at our firehouse studio years ago. Page 2 More than 70 years after the kidnapping, torture and lynching of 14-year-old Emmett Till in Mississippi, a major new photography exhibit and companion book ask how the world would be different “If Emmett Till Lived.” The Black teenager’s brutal murder, as well as his open-casket funeral that displayed his mutilated body, shocked the United States in 1955 and became a galvanizing moment in the civil rights movement. If Till had lived, he would be just over 85 years old today. “Art really is one of the critical modes of creating an appeal to the moral imagination,” says historian Sarah Elizabeth Lewis, the curator behind “If Emmett Till Lived” and editor of the book. Lewis collaborated on the project with Till’s surviving cousin, Reverend Wheeler Parker Jr., the last living witness to see Till alive. The exhibit opens at the Museum of Contemporary Photography at Columbia College Chicago on September 10.

articles.title: Johanna Fernández Dies at 55: Leading Scholar on the Young Lords & Latinx Freedom Movement
articles.content: We look at the life and legacy of Dominican American historian, activist and prison abolitionist Dr. Johanna Fernández, who died on July 30 after a long battle with cancer. She was 55 years old. As a professor of history at Baruch College and the CUNY Graduate Center, Fernández was a leading scholar of the Young Lords, the radical 1960s civil rights organization founded in Chicago and New York and modeled on the Black Panthers. Fernández also created the Latinx Freedom Movement Archive and Exhibition Project, alongside historian Felipe Hinojosa. The exhibition is currently on view at The Shed in New York City, as well as in Chicago and Los Angeles. Iterations will also be presented in Houston and Washington, D.C. Democracy Now! co-host Juan González, who was a founding member of the Young Lords before his career in journalism, remembers Fernández as “a consummate historian,” as well as a committed activist who devoted herself to advancing social justice. “She was an amazing person with enormous energy and spirit, and we are all better people for having known her,” he says.
